chunks: My father narrated (may God be pleased with him) that Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashim narrated from his father, from Al-Hussein ibn Al-Hasan Al-Farsi, from Suleiman ibn Hafs Al-Basri, from Abdullah ibn Al-Hussein ibn Zayd ibn Ali ibn Al-Hussein ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon them), from his father, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his forefathers, from Ali (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said:

Indeed, God, the Mighty and Majestic, when He created Paradise, created it from two adobes: one of gold and one of silver. He made its walls ruby, its ceiling chrysolite, its pebbles pearls, and its soil saffron and fine musk. Then He said to it, 'Speak,' so it said, 'There is no god but You, the Everlasting, the Sustainer. Blessed is he who enters me.' Then God, the Mighty and Majestic, said, 'By My Glory, My Majesty, My Grandeur, and My Exaltation, the alcoholics, the drunkards, the tale-bearers (who are slanderers), the effeminate men (who are pimps), the detectives (who are eavesdroppers), the effeminate (hermaphrodites), the grave-robbers, the tax-collectors, those who sever ties of kinship, and the Qadarites shall not enter it.'
ai.seo_question: Who are the specific groups of people that will not enter Paradise according to this hadith?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq presents this cosmological narrative to illustrate the divine grandeur of Paradise, personifying it as a witness to God's majesty before enumerating the exclusions. The hadith highlights specific moral and social vices—such as slander (al-namm) and severing kinship (qati' al-rahim)—that are particularly emphasized in Shia tradition as barriers to spiritual elevation. This account serves as a theological reminder that entry into Paradise is contingent not only on faith but also on the purification of character from these specific sins.
